content: Pseudomonas syringae is a rod-shaped, Gram-negative bacterium equipped with polar flagella. It belongs to the genus Pseudomonas and has been classified within the Pseudomonas syringae group based on 16S rRNA analysis. This bacterium is a plant pathogen capable of infecting a wide variety of plant species and exists in over 50 different pathovars. Historically, many of these pathovars were considered separate species within the Pseudomonas genus, but molecular biology techniques, such as DNA hybridization, have demonstrated that they all belong to the Pseudomonas syringae species. The bacterium was named after the lilac tree (Syringa vulgaris), from which it was first isolated. Pseudomonas syringae is negative for arginine dihydrolase and oxidase activity and produces the polymer levan when grown on sucrose nutrient agar. It secretes a lipopeptide plant toxin called syringomycin and exhibits a yellow fluorescent appearance when cultured in vitro on King’s B medium due to the production of the siderophore pyoverdin. Additionally, it possesses ice-nucleating properties. Epidemiology The development of disease caused by Pseudomonas syringae is favored by wet and cool environmental conditions, with optimal temperatures for disease ranging from 12°C to 25°C, although this can vary depending on the specific pathovar. While it is primarily a plant pathogen, Pseudomonas syringae can also survive as a saprophyte in the phyllosphere under conditions unfavorable for disease. Some saprophytic strains of Pseudomonas syringae have been utilized as biocontrol agents to combat post-harvest rots. Pathovars Following ribotypical analysis, several pathovars of Pseudomonas syringae were reclassified into other species, such as Pseudomonas amygdali, Pseudomonas tomato, Pseudomonas coronafaciens, Pseudomonas avellanae, Pseudomonas helianthi, Pseudomonas tremae, Pseudomonas cannabina, and Pseudomonas viridiflava. The remaining pathovars include: Pseudomonas syringae pv. aceris: Infects maple (Acer species). Pseudomonas syringae pv. aptata: Infects beets (Beta vulgaris). Pseudomonas syringae pv. atrofaciens: Infects wheat (Triticum aestivum). Pseudomonas syringae pv. dysoxyli: Infects the kohekohe tree (Dysoxylum spectabile). Pseudomonas syringae pv. japonica: Infects barley (Hordeum vulgare). Pseudomonas syringae pv. lapsa: Infects wheat (Triticum aestivum). Pseudomonas syringae pv. panici: Infects Panicum grass species. Pseudomonas syringae pv. papulans: Infects crabapple (Malus sylvestris species). Pseudomonas syringae pv. pisi: Infects peas (Pisum sativum). Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae: Infects Syringa and Phaseolus species. It is worth noting that Pseudomonas savastanoi was previously considered a pathovar or subspecies of Pseudomonas syringae and is still often referred to as Pseudomonas syringae pv. savastanoi. However, DNA-relatedness studies have established it as a distinct species. Pseudomonas savastanoi itself has three host-specific pathovars: fraxini, which causes ash canker; nerii, which infects oleander; and oleae, which causes olive knot. Genome Sequencing Projects The genomes of several strains of Pseudomonas syringae have been sequenced, including Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000, Pseudomonas syringae pv. syringae B728a, and Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola 1448A.
